props.title: The Man Who Came to Dinner
props.initialSlug: Cranky critic wreaks havoc as unwanted houseguest

sections.content: **The Man Who Came to Dinner** (1942) represents the pinnacle of rapid-fire theatrical adaptations from Hollywood's Golden Age. Based on the hit Broadway play by Moss Hart and George S. Kaufman, it showcases Monty Woolley recreating his stage role as acerbic radio personality Sheridan Whiteside. The film's influence echoes through later caustic comedies like **All About Eve** (1950) and **My Man Godfrey** (1936), establishing a template for sharp-tongued wit delivered at machine-gun pace. Director William Keighley captures the theatrical energy while opening up the play just enough for cinema, similar to how Howard Hawks would later approach **Arsenic and Old Lace** (1944).

sections.content: The film's greatest strength lies in its constellation of character actors, with Bette Davis deliberately taking a supporting role as Whiteside's secretary Maggie Cutler. This ensemble approach influenced later theatrical adaptations like **The Philadelphia Story** (1940) and **Born Yesterday** (1950), where the interplay between characters matters more than star power. The confined setting - mostly in the Stanley family's living room - creates a pressure cooker for the comedy, anticipating single-location films like **Rope** (1948) and **12 Angry Men** (1957).

Screenwriter Julius and Philip Epstein maintained much of the original play's topical references while adding cinematic flourishes. Their work here preceded their famous collaboration on **Casablanca** (1942), showing similar skill at balancing multiple character arcs and weaving quotable dialogue. The film's structure - with Whiteside manipulating everyone from his wheelchair command center - created a template for later "puppet master" characters like Addison DeWitt in **All About Eve** (1950). sections.content: The success of **The Man Who Came to Dinner** (1942) helped establish Warner Bros.' house style for sophisticated comedy, influencing films like **Watch on the Rhine** (1943) and **The Voice of the Turtle** (1947). The film's preservation of theatrical timing while adding cinematic elements created a blueprint for adapting stage works, visible in later successes like **Harvey** (1950) and **The Seven Year Itch** (1955).
